lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
Most vectors change direction when you multiply them by a matrix. **Eigenvectors** are the special directions that do not: the matrix only stretches them. That is why eigenvectors reveal the structure of a matrix. In data science they give the principal components of a data set (eigenvectors of the covariance matrix), the long-run behaviour of Markov chains and ranking algorithms such as PageRank, and the stability of learning dynamics.

> [!ghi-nho] To find eigenvalues, solve $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. To find eigenvectors, solve $(A-\lambda I)v=0$. To diagonalize, collect $n$ independent eigenvectors as the columns of $P$.

:::Predict before you read
Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $A(1,0)^\top$, $A(0,1)^\top$ and $A(1,1)^\top$. Which of the three vectors keep their direction? Check your answer in the first section.
:::

sections.title: What an eigenvector is

parts.title: Definition
parts.md:
An **eigenvector** of a square matrix $A$ is a **nonzero** vector $v$ such that

$$Av=\lambda v$$

The scalar $\lambda$ is the **eigenvalue**. Multiplying by $A$ stretches $v$ by $\lambda$ (and reverses it if $\lambda<0$), but does not turn it.

parts.title: A first example
parts.md:
Take $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$.

$$A\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=2\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad A\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}=3\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$$

The first two vectors keep their direction (eigenvectors); $(1,1)$ is turned, so it is not an eigenvector.

parts.title: The characteristic equation
parts.md:
Rewrite $Av=\lambda v$ as $(A-\lambda I)v=0$. A nonzero $v$ exists exactly when $A-\lambda I$ is singular, that is

$$\det(A-\lambda I)=0$$

This is the **characteristic equation**; its roots are the eigenvalues. For each eigenvalue, the eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of $(A-\lambda I)v=0$.

sections.intro: Most vectors change direction when you multiply them by a matrix. Eigenvectors are the special directions that do not.
sections.outro:
> [!ghi-nho] Only $v\neq0$ is required. The eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ is allowed (it happens exactly when $A$ is singular), and an eigenvector may have zero coordinates and any length.

**Back to the prediction:** $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ keep their direction; $(1,1)$ does not.

sections.title: Worked example: a 2 × 2 matrix

parts.title: Form A − λI
parts.md: $$A-\lambda I=\begin{pmatrix}4-\lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda\end{pmatrix}$$

parts.title: Write the characteristic equation
parts.md:
$$\det(A-\lambda I)=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=(\lambda-2)(\lambda-5)=0$$

The eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=2$.

parts.title: Eigenvectors for λ = 5
parts.md:
$$A-5I=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$$

Both rows say $-x+y=0$, so $y=x$ and $v=t\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $t\neq0$.

parts.title: Eigenvectors for λ = 2
parts.md:
$$A-2I=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$$

Both rows say $2x+y=0$, so $y=-2x$ and $v=t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, $t\neq0$.

parts.title: Check Av = λv
parts.md:
$$A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\5\end{pmatrix}=5\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad A\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-4\end{pmatrix}=2\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$$

Always check: it takes seconds and catches every sign error.

parts.title: Sanity check
parts.md: The eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant: $5+2=7=4+3$ and $5\cdot2=10=\det A$.

sections.intro: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

sections.title: Worked example: a 3 × 3 matrix

parts.title: Form A − λI and expand
parts.md:
$$\det(A-\lambda I)=\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda&2&-2\\1&2-\lambda&1\\-1&-1&-\lambda\end{vmatrix}$$

Expanding along row 1 gives

$$(1-\lambda)(\lambda^2-2\lambda+1)-2(1-\lambda)-2(1-\lambda)=(1-\lambda)\bigl[(\lambda-1)^2-4\bigr]$$

parts.title: Factor
parts.md:
$$(\lambda-1)^2-4=(\lambda-3)(\lambda+1)\ \Rightarrow\ \det(A-\lambda I)=-(\lambda-1)(\lambda+1)(\lambda-3)$$

The eigenvalues are $1,\ -1,\ 3$.

parts.title: Eigenvectors for λ = 1
parts.md:
$$A-I=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$$

The first two equations are $2y-2z=0$ and $x+y+z=0$. So $y=z$ and $x=-2z$:

$$v=t\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},\ t\neq0$$

The third equation is the negative of the second and adds nothing.

parts.title: Eigenvectors for λ = −1
parts.md:
$$A+I=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$$

The first equation gives $x+y-z=0$; subtracting it from $x+3y+z=0$ gives $2y+2z=0$. So $y=-z$ and $x=2z$:

$$v=t\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},\ t\neq0$$

parts.title: Eigenvectors for λ = 3
parts.md:
$$A-3I=\begin{pmatrix}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -3\end{pmatrix}$$

The first equation is $x-y+z=0$ and the third is $-x-y-3z=0$. Substituting $x=y-z$ gives $-2y-2z=0$, so $y=-z$ and $x=-2z$:

$$v=t\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},\ t\neq0$$

parts.title: Check each pair
parts.md:
$$A\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad A\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=-1\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad A\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-3\\3\end{pmatrix}=3\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$$

Trace check: $1+(-1)+3=3=1+2+0$. Determinant check: $1\cdot(-1)\cdot3=-3=\det A$.

sections.intro: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$.

sections.title: Facts that save time

parts.title: Diagonal and triangular matrices
parts.md: The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries. For $\operatorname{diag}(-2,0,5)$ they are $-2,\ 0,\ 5$ and the standard basis vectors are eigenvectors.

parts.title: Trace and determinant
parts.md: The sum of the eigenvalues is the trace; their product is the determinant. Use this to catch arithmetic errors.

parts.title: Zero eigenvalue
parts.md: $\lambda=0$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $A$ is singular ($\det A=0$).

parts.title: Powers, inverses, polynomials
parts.md: If $Av=\lambda v$ then $A^kv=\lambda^kv$, $p(A)v=p(\lambda)v$ for any polynomial $p$, and, when $A$ is invertible, $A^{-1}v=\lambda^{-1}v$ (same eigenvector, reciprocal eigenvalue).

parts.title: Distinct eigenvalues
parts.md: Eigenvectors that belong to **distinct** eigenvalues are linearly independent.

sections.intro: Five facts that avoid long computations.

sections.title: Eigenvectors as a coordinate system

parts.title: Independence and basis
parts.md: Vectors $v_1,\dots,v_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are **linearly independent** when $c_1v_1+\dots+c_nv_n=0$ forces every $c_j=0$. An independent list of $n$ vectors is a **basis**: every vector has a unique expression as their combination, and the matrix with these columns is invertible.

parts.title: Diagonalization
parts.md: A real matrix $A$ is **diagonalizable** over $\mathbb{R}$ if $A=PDP^{-1}$ for an invertible real $P$ and a real diagonal $D$. The columns of $P$ are eigenvectors and the matching diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues.

parts.title: Why the column rule works
parts.md: Put $P=[v_1\cdots v_n]$ and $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$. Then $AP=[Av_1\cdots Av_n]=[\lambda_1v_1\cdots\lambda_nv_n]=PD$. If $P$ is invertible, $A=PDP^{-1}$. **Column order and eigenvalue order must agree.**

parts.title: Powers become easy
parts.md: $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$ with $D^k=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n^k)$. This is why eigen-decompositions are used to study repeated transformations such as Markov chains.

sections.intro: A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

sections.title: Worked example: diagonalization and powers

parts.title: Eigenvalues
parts.md:
Expand along row 1:

$$\det(B-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)\bigl[(3-\lambda)(9-\lambda)-16\bigr]=(2-\lambda)(\lambda^2-12\lambda+11)=(2-\lambda)(\lambda-1)(\lambda-11)$$

The eigenvalues are $1,\ 2,\ 11$.

parts.title: Eigenvectors
parts.md: $$\lambda=1:\ \begin{cases}x=0\\y=-2z\end{cases}\Rightarrow v_1=(0,-2,1)^\top;\qquad \lambda=2:\ y=z=0\Rightarrow v_2=(1,0,0)^\top;\qquad \lambda=11:\ \begin{cases}x=0\\z=2y\end{cases}\Rightarrow v_3=(0,1,2)^\top$$

parts.title: Build P and D in the same order
parts.md:
$$P=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix},\qquad D=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 11\end{pmatrix}$$

$\det P=5\neq0$, so $P$ is invertible. Column $j$ of $P$ goes with entry $j$ of $D$.

parts.title: Check BP = PD
parts.md:
$$BP=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 11 \\ 1 & 0 & 22\end{pmatrix}=PD$$

The columns of $BP$ are $1\cdot v_1,\ 2\cdot v_2,\ 11\cdot v_3$.

parts.title: Invert P
parts.md: $$P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -\tfrac{2}{5} & \tfrac{1}{5} \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{5} & \tfrac{2}{5}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=PDP^{-1}$$

parts.title: Powers
parts.md:
$$B^2=P\operatorname{diag}(1,4,121)P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 25 & 48 \\ 0 & 48 & 97\end{pmatrix}$$

For every $k\ge0$, $B^k=P\operatorname{diag}(1,2^k,11^k)P^{-1}$. For instance, $(B^k)_{22}=(-2)(1)(-\tfrac25)+(1)(11^k)(\tfrac15)=\dfrac{4+11^k}{5}$. Check: $k=1$ gives $3=B_{22}$ and $k=2$ gives $25$, as in $B^2$.

sections.intro: Diagonalize $B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 9\end{pmatrix}$ and use it to find $B^k$.

sections.title: When diagonalization works and when it fails

parts.title: It works
parts.md:
- $n$ **distinct** real eigenvalues: always diagonalizable.
- A repeated eigenvalue can still work: for $2I_2$ every nonzero vector is an eigenvector for $\lambda=2$, so two independent eigenvectors exist.

parts.title: It fails
parts.md:
$$J=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$$

$\lambda=2$ is repeated, and $(J-2I)v=0\iff y=0$, so all eigenvectors lie on **one** line. There is no eigenvector basis: $J$ is not diagonalizable although its eigenvalue is real.

sections.intro: Count independent eigenvectors, not eigenvalues.
sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] Repeated eigenvalues neither guarantee nor rule out diagonalization; you must check them separately. A real matrix can also fail to have real eigenvalues at all (for example a rotation by $90^\circ$ has $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2+1$), and then it is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$.

sections.title: Find the error in this solution

parts.md:
A classmate diagonalizes $B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 9\end{pmatrix}$ with the eigenvectors $v_1=(0,-2,1)^\top$ ($\lambda=1$), $v_2=(1,0,0)^\top$ ($\lambda=2$), $v_3=(0,1,2)^\top$ ($\lambda=11$).

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 1.** $P=[v_1\ v_2\ v_3]=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 2.** Reading the factors of $(2-\lambda)(\lambda-1)(\lambda-11)$ from left to right, the eigenvalues are $2, 1, 11$, so $D=\operatorname{diag}(2,1,11)$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 3.** Therefore $B=PDP^{-1}$.

:::Which step is wrong?
**Step 2.** The order of the diagonal entries must match the order of the columns of $P$. Column 1 of $P$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda=1$, so $d_1=1$, not $2$. Test the first column: $Bv_1=(0,-2,1)^\top=1\cdot v_1$, but column 1 of $PD$ with the wrong $D$ is $2v_1=(0,-4,2)^\top$. So $BP\neq PD$. The correct choice is $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,11)$.
:::

**Principal component analysis.** A covariance matrix such as $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric. Its eigenvectors are the directions of the data cloud and its eigenvalues are the variances along them:

$$\Sigma\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=3\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Sigma\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=1\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$$

The direction $(1,1)$ carries variance $3$, the largest, so it is the first principal component.

**Repeated transformations.** Because $A^kv=\lambda^kv$, repeated application of $A$ is dominated by the eigenvalue of largest absolute value. This is the idea behind power iteration and PageRank, and it decides whether a linear dynamical system grows, shrinks or stays bounded.

parts.title: Can an eigenvalue be $0$?
parts.md: Yes. It happens exactly when $A$ is singular. Only the eigenvector must be nonzero.

parts.title: Can an eigenvector be the zero vector?
parts.md: No: $A\cdot0=\lambda\cdot0$ holds for every $\lambda$, so allowing $0$ would make every number an eigenvalue.

parts.title: Are eigenvectors unique?
parts.md: Only up to a nonzero multiple: if $v$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda$, so is $tv$ for every $t\neq0$. The eigenvectors for one eigenvalue (together with $0$) form a subspace.

parts.title: Does a repeated eigenvalue mean $A$ is not diagonalizable?
parts.md: Not necessarily. $2I_2$ has the repeated eigenvalue $2$ and is diagonal. Count the independent eigenvectors for each eigenvalue.

Check the eigenvalue computations. `numpy.linalg.eig` returns the eigenvalues and a matrix whose **columns** are eigenvectors, normalised to length 1. They match the hand computation up to order and scaling. ```html 
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2, -2],
              [1, 2,  1],
              [-1, -1, 0]], dtype=float)

vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
vals, vecs = np.real_if_close(vals), np.real_if_close(vecs)   # drop zero imaginary parts
print("eigenvalues:", np.round(vals, 6))     # the order is not guaranteed
print(np.round(vecs, 4))                     # columns are unit-length eigenvectors
for lam, v in zip(vals, vecs.T):
    print(np.allclose(A @ v, lam * v))   # A v = lambda v
``` **Output** ```html 
eigenvalues: [ 3. -1.  1.]
[[-0.8165 -0.8165 -0.8165]
 [-0.4082  0.4082  0.4082]
 [ 0.4082 -0.4082  0.4082]]
True
True
True
``` Exact diagonalization with `sympy`. The columns of `P` may be ordered or scaled differently from ours, but `P * D * P**-1` is always `B`. ```html 
import sympy as sp

B = sp.Matrix([[2, 0, 0], [0, 3, 4], [0, 4, 9]])
P, D = B.diagonalize()            # B = P D P^{-1}
print("P =", P)
print("D =", D)
print("P D P^-1 == B:", P * D * P.inv() == B)

# powers: compare (B^n)[1, 1] with (4 + 11^n)/5
print("(B^n)[1,1]:", [(B**n)[1, 1] for n in (1, 2, 3)])
print("(4 + 11^n)/5:", [sp.Rational(4 + 11**n, 5) for n in (1, 2, 3)])
``` **Output** ```html 
P = Matrix([[0, 1, 0], [-2, 0, 1], [1, 0, 2]])
D = Matrix([[1, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, 0, 11]])
P D P^-1 == B: True
(B^n)[1,1]: [3, 25, 267]
(4 + 11^n)/5: [3, 25, 267]
```

items.meaning: A nonzero v with Av = λv. Nothing else is required: λ may be 0 and v may have zero entries and any length.
det(A − λI) = 0. Its roots are the eigenvalues; for each, solve (A − λI)v = 0 for the eigenvectors.
The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
Sum of eigenvalues = trace; product of eigenvalues = det A. Use them as a check.
If Av = λv then Aᵏv = λᵏv, p(A)v = p(λ)v and, for invertible A, A⁻¹v = λ⁻¹v.
A = PDP⁻¹ with P invertible and D diagonal. Equivalent: A has n linearly independent eigenvectors.
Columns of P are eigenvectors; D has the matching eigenvalues in the same order (AP = PD).
items.note: Column order and eigenvalue order must agree.

items.meaning: Repeated eigenvalues may give too few eigenvectors. [[2, 1], [0, 2]] has one eigenvector line and is not diagonalizable; 2I is.
Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ with Dᵏ = diag(λ₁ᵏ, …, λₙᵏ).

summary: An eigenvector v ≠ 0 of A satisfies Av = λv: A only stretches it by the eigenvalue λ.
Eigenvalues are the roots of det(A − λI) = 0; eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of (A − λI)v = 0. Always check Av = λv.
Diagonal and triangular matrices have their diagonal entries as eigenvalues; eigenvalues add to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
A is diagonalizable exactly when it has n independent eigenvectors; then A = PDP⁻¹ with D in the same order as the columns of P.
Powers and polynomials of A act on eigenvectors by powers and polynomials of λ, so Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $v = (-2, 1, 1)^\top$, which value satisfies $Av = \lambda v$?
questions.explanation: Multiplying gives $Av=(1\cdot(-2)+2\cdot1-2\cdot1,\ 1\cdot(-2)+2\cdot1+1\cdot1,\ (-1)(-2)+(-1)(1)+0)=(-2,1,1)^\top=1\cdot v$. Since $v\neq0$, the eigenvalue is $1$. The other numbers give a different vector. (Note that $3$ and $-1$ are eigenvalues of $A$, but with other eigenvectors.)

questions.prompt: Which condition is part of the definition of an eigenvector $v$?
questions.explanation: An eigenvector must be nonzero, because $A\cdot 0=\lambda\cdot 0$ holds for every $\lambda$ and would make the idea meaningless. Nothing else is required: coordinates may be zero, any length is allowed, and the eigenvalue may be $0$ (exactly when $A$ is singular).

questions.prompt: What is the set of eigenvalues of $D = \operatorname{diag}(-2, 0, 5)$?
questions.explanation: For a diagonal matrix each standard basis vector $e_j$ is an eigenvector, and its eigenvalue is the $j$-th diagonal entry. So the eigenvalues are $-2$, $0$ and $5$, with their signs.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is invertible and $Av = -2v$ with $v \neq 0$, which statement holds?
questions.explanation: Multiply $Av=-2v$ by $A^{-1}$ to get $v=-2A^{-1}v$, and divide by $-2$: $A^{-1}v=-\tfrac12 v$. Inversion replaces a nonzero eigenvalue by its reciprocal and keeps the eigenvector.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, which gives all eigenvectors for $\lambda = -1$, with $t \neq 0$?
questions.explanation: Solve $(A+I)v=0$. The rows give $x+y-z=0$ and $x+3y+z=0$ (the third row repeats the first). Subtracting gives $2y+2z=0$, so $y=-z$ and then $x=z-y=2z$. Every eigenvector is $t(2,-1,1)^\top$. Check: $A(2,-1,1)^\top=(-2,1,-1)^\top=-1\cdot(2,-1,1)^\top$. Option B is an eigenvector for $\lambda=1$ and option D for $\lambda=3$.

questions.prompt: For $B = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 9\end{pmatrix}$, choose $P = [(0,-2,1)^\top\ (1,0,0)^\top\ (0,1,2)^\top]$. Which $D$ satisfies $B = PDP^{-1}$?
questions.explanation: Compute $B$ times each column: $B(0,-2,1)^\top=(0,-2,1)^\top$ (eigenvalue $1$), $B(1,0,0)^\top=2\cdot(1,0,0)^\top$ (eigenvalue $2$) and $B(0,1,2)^\top=(0,11,22)^\top=11\cdot(0,1,2)^\top$ (eigenvalue $11$). So $BP=P\operatorname{diag}(1,2,11)$, and $P$ is invertible because its columns are independent ($\det P=5$). The diagonal order must match the column order.

questions.prompt: For which real $t$ is $A_t = \begin{pmatrix}2 & t & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$?
questions.explanation: If $t=0$ the matrix is already diagonal. If $t\neq0$, solving $(A_t-2I)v=0$ forces $y=0$ and $z=0$, so the eigenvalue $2$ has only one independent eigenvector $(1,0,0)^\top$; the eigenvalue $3$ contributes only $e_3$. That is two independent eigenvectors for a $3\times3$ matrix, so there is no eigenvector basis and no diagonalization.

questions.prompt: Let $B = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 9\end{pmatrix}$. For every positive integer $k$, what is $(B^k)_{23}$?
questions.explanation: Use $B^k=P\operatorname{diag}(1,2^k,11^k)P^{-1}$. Row 2 of $P$ is $(-2,0,1)$ and column 3 of $P^{-1}$ is $(\tfrac15,0,\tfrac25)^\top$, so $(B^k)_{23}=(-2)(1)(\tfrac15)+0+(1)(11^k)(\tfrac25)=\dfrac{2(11^k-1)}{5}$. Check at $k=1$: $\frac{2\cdot10}{5}=4$, the original entry $B_{23}$. At $k=2$ it gives $48$, which matches $(B^2)_{23}$.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, which is the complete solution set of $(A^2 - I_3)x = 0$, with $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$?
questions.explanation: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1,-1,3$ with an eigenvector basis, and $(A^2-I)v=(\lambda^2-1)v$ for an eigenvector. The polynomial $\lambda^2-1$ vanishes at $1$ and $-1$ but not at $3$, so the kernel is spanned by $(-2,1,1)^\top$ and $(2,-1,1)^\top$, which is the plane $x_1=-2x_2$ with $x_3$ free. Directly: $A^2-I$ has rows $(4,8,0)$, $(2,4,0)$, $(-2,-4,0)$, i.e. the single condition $x_1+2x_2=0$.

questions.prompt: Find the **larger** eigenvalue of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: $\det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)(-2-\lambda)-4=\lambda^2+\lambda-6=(\lambda+3)(\lambda-2)$, so the eigenvalues are $-3$ and $2$. The larger one is $2$. (Check: trace $-1=-3+2$ and determinant $-6=(-3)(2)$.)

questions.prompt: A matrix with a repeated eigenvalue is never diagonalizable.
questions.explanation: False. $2I_2$ has the repeated eigenvalue $2$ and is already diagonal. Diagonalizability depends on whether there are $n$ independent eigenvectors, not on whether the eigenvalues repeat. ($\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ is a repeated-eigenvalue matrix that is not diagonalizable.)

questions.prompt: If $0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, then $A$ is invertible.
questions.explanation: False. $Av=0\cdot v=0$ with $v\neq 0$ means $A$ sends a nonzero vector to $0$, so $A$ is singular. A square matrix is invertible exactly when $0$ is **not** an eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for diagonalizing an $n\times n$ matrix in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Eigenvalues first; then eigenvectors for each; check that there are $n$ independent ones (otherwise stop: not diagonalizable); then assemble $P$ and $D$ in the same order; finally verify $AP=PD$.
sequence: Solve det(A − λI) = 0 for the eigenvalues
Check that you have n linearly independent eigenvectors
Put the eigenvectors in the columns of P and the eigenvalues in the same order on the diagonal of D

questions.prompt: $Av=3v$ with $v\neq 0$. Then $(A^2+2A+I)v=\mu v$. Enter $\mu$.
questions.explanation: $A^2v=3^2v=9v$ and $2Av=6v$, so $(A^2+2A+I)v=(9+6+1)v=16v$. In general $p(A)v=p(\lambda)v$ with $p(\lambda)=\lambda^2+2\lambda+1=(\lambda+1)^2=16$.

lessons.title: Topic 5 · Vector Spaces and Linear Mappings
lessons.description: Vector-space axioms, the main examples (Rⁿ, matrices, functions), subspaces, linear mappings, standard matrices, affine maps, and inverses of linear maps.
objectives: State the vector-space axioms and decide which one fails for a proposed set with its operations
Compute sums, scalar multiples and zero vectors in Rⁿ, in spaces of matrices and in C(ℝ)
Apply the subspace test and explain which of its three conditions a set fails
Test whether a map is linear using additivity, homogeneity and the quick test T(0) = 0
Construct the standard matrix of a linear map from a formula or from its values on a basis, and evaluate T from it
Distinguish linear from affine maps, compose maps, and find the inverse of a linear map via its matrix
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
Linear algebra is not only about columns of numbers. Matrices and functions can be added and scaled in exactly the same way, so the same ideas apply to them: they are all **vectors** in a **vector space**. A **linear map** is a function between vector spaces that respects addition and scaling, and in $\mathbb{R}^n$ every such map is a matrix. That is how data science sees a model: each layer of a neural network is a linear map plus a shift followed by a nonlinearity, and PCA is a projection, itself a linear map.

> [!ghi-nho] A map $T$ is linear if taking a linear combination before applying $T$ gives the same result as taking it afterwards: $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$.

:::Predict before you read
Is $T(x,y)=(x+1,\ y)$ linear? It looks very simple. Compute $T(0,0)$ and decide, then check your reasoning in the worked example on linear maps.
:::

sections.title: The ten axioms in four groups

parts.title: Addition
parts.md: For $u,v,w\in V$: closure $u+v\in V$; commutativity $u+v=v+u$; associativity $u+(v+w)=(u+v)+w$.

parts.title: Zero and negatives
parts.md: There is a **zero vector** $0_V$ with $u+0_V=u$ for every $u$; every $u$ has a negative $-u$ with $u+(-u)=0_V$.

parts.title: Scaling
parts.md: For scalars $c,d\in\mathbb{R}$: closure $cu\in V$; $c(du)=(cd)u$; and $1u=u$.

parts.title: Distributive laws
parts.md: $c(u+v)=cu+cv$ and $(c+d)u=cu+du$.

sections.intro: A **real vector space** is a nonempty set $V$ with addition of vectors and multiplication by real scalars that obey ten rules. A 'vector' is then any element of such a set: an arrow, a column of numbers, a matrix, a function.
sections.outro: These rules imply $0u=0_V$, $c\,0_V=0_V$ and $(-1)u=-u$. To show that something is **not** a vector space, find one rule that fails.

sections.title: Three families of vector spaces

parts.title: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$
parts.md: Addition and scaling are componentwise: $(1,2)+(3,-1)=(4,1)$ and $2(1,2)=(2,4)$. The zero vector is $(0,\dots,0)$.

parts.title: Matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$
parts.md: Fix the shape $m\times n$ and use matrix addition and scalar multiplication. The zero vector is the zero matrix of that shape.

parts.title: Continuous functions $C(\mathbb{R})$
parts.md:
Operations are pointwise: $(f+g)(t)=f(t)+g(t)$ and $(cf)(t)=c\,f(t)$. The zero vector is the function that is $0$ for every $t$, and the negative of $f$ is $-f$.

For $f(t)=t^2$ and $g(t)=1-t$:

$$(3f-2g)(t)=3t^2-2(1-t)=3t^2+2t-2$$

sections.intro: The same ten rules cover all three.
sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] The zero vector of $C(\mathbb{R})$ is the function $0$, **not** the constant function $1$. The zero vector must leave every function unchanged under addition.

sections.title: Worked example: the subspace test

parts.title: Closed under scaling?
parts.md: For $(x,y)\in W$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$: $cx+cy=c(x+y)=c\cdot0=0$, so $c(x,y)\in W$.

parts.title: Conclusion
parts.md: All three conditions hold, so $W$ is a subspace. Geometrically it is the line $y=-x$ through the origin.

sections.intro: A subset $W$ of a vector space is a **subspace** if it contains $0$ and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; the other axioms are inherited. Is $W=\{(x,y):x+y=0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ a subspace?

sections.title: Three ways a set can fail the test

parts.title: No zero vector
parts.md: $\{(x,y):x+y=1\}$ is a line that misses the origin, so $0\notin W$. This is the quickest check.

parts.title: Not closed under scaling
parts.md: $\{(x,y):x\ge0\}$ contains $0$ and is closed under addition, but $(-1)\cdot(1,0)=(-1,0)$ leaves the set.

parts.title: Not closed under addition
parts.md: $\{(x,y):xy=0\}$ (the two axes) contains $0$ and is closed under scaling, but $(1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1)$ has $xy=1\neq0$.

sections.intro: Each of the three conditions can fail on its own, so you must check all three.
sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] Every subspace contains $0$; failing that single test already settles the question.

sections.title: Worked example: is the map linear?

parts.title: Quick necessary test
parts.md: Compute $T(0)$. If it is not $0$, stop: $T$ is not linear. If it is $0$, you still have to check the two conditions.

parts.title: Homogeneity for $S$
parts.md:
$$S(cu)=(cx_1+cy_1,\ 2cx_1-cy_1)=c\,(x_1+y_1,\ 2x_1-y_1)=cS(u)$$

Both conditions hold for all $u,v,c$, so $S$ is linear.

parts.title: A map that fails homogeneity
parts.md:
$R(x,y)=(xy,\ x)$ has $R(0)=0$ but

$$R(2,2)=(4,2)\quad\text{while}\quad 2R(1,1)=2(1,1)=(2,2)$$

One counterexample is enough: $R$ is not linear.

parts.title: A translation
parts.md: $T(x,y)=(x,\ y+2)$ has $T(0,0)=(0,2)\neq(0,0)$, so it is not linear.

sections.intro: A map $T:V\to W$ is **linear** if $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$ (additivity) and $T(cu)=cT(u)$ (homogeneity) for all vectors and scalars. Equivalently $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$. Every linear map sends $0$ to $0$.
sections.outro: **Back to the prediction:** $T(x,y)=(x+1,y)$ looks simple but $T(0,0)=(1,0)\neq 0$, so it is not linear. Every matrix map $x\mapsto Ax$ is linear because $A(u+v)=Au+Av$ and $A(cu)=cAu$.

sections.title: Worked example: the standard matrix of a linear map

parts.title: Apply T to the basis vectors
Use them as columns
parts.md:
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$$

Why: the images are the **columns**, not the rows.

parts.title: Test it
parts.md: $T(1,2)=(2-2,\ 1+6)=(0,7)$ and $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\7\end{pmatrix}$. Both agree.

parts.title: A map given by its values on a basis
parts.md:
A linear $T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^3$ with $T(e_1)=(1,0,2)$ and $T(e_2)=(0,1,-1)$ has the $3\times2$ matrix

$$\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$$

and $T(3,-2)=3T(e_1)-2T(e_2)=(3,0,6)+(0,-2,2)=(3,-2,8)$. Knowing $T$ on a basis determines $T$ everywhere.

sections.intro: Every linear map $T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ is multiplication by a matrix, the **standard matrix** $A=[T(e_1)\ \cdots\ T(e_n)]$. The reason: $x=\sum_j x_je_j$, so $T(x)=\sum_j x_jT(e_j)=Ax$. Build the matrix of $T(x,y)=(2x-y,\ x+3y)$.
sections.outro: A map $T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ has an $m\times n$ matrix.

sections.title: Linear versus affine maps

parts.title: Linear: $x\mapsto Ax$
parts.md:
- Sends $0$ to $0$.
- Preserves linear combinations: $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$.

parts.title: Affine: $x\mapsto Ax+b$
parts.md:
- $T(0)=b$, so it is linear **exactly when $b=0$**.
- A translation $x\mapsto x+b$ with $b\neq0$ is the basic nonlinear example.

sections.intro: A fully connected layer of a neural network computes $x\mapsto Wx+b$ followed by a nonlinear function. The $Wx$ part is linear; adding the bias $b$ makes the map affine, and the activation function makes the whole thing nonlinear.

sections.title: Worked example: composition and inverse

parts.title: Compose
parts.md:
$S\circ T$ means: apply $T$ first, then $S$. Its matrix is the product with the rightmost factor acting first:

$$BA=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$$

Check: $S(T(x,y))=S(2x+y,\ x+y)=(3x+2y,\ x+y)$.

parts.title: Is T invertible?
parts.md: $\det A=2\cdot1-1\cdot1=1\neq0$, so $A$ is invertible and so is $T$. The matrix of $T^{-1}$ is $A^{-1}$.

parts.title: Compute $A^{-1}$
parts.md: $$A^{-1}=\frac11\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$$

parts.title: Solve $T(v)=(3,2)$
parts.md:
$$T^{-1}(3,2)=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3-2\\-3+4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$$

Check: $T(1,1)=(2+1,\ 1+1)=(3,2)$. Applying $T$ to your answer must give back the input.

sections.intro: Let $T(x,y)=(2x+y,\ x+y)$ and $S(x,y)=(x+y,\ y)$. Their matrices are $A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.

sections.title: Find the error in this solution

parts.md:
On $C(\mathbb{R})$ define $(Sf)(t)=f(t)+1$. A classmate claims $S$ is linear:

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 1.** $S(f+g)(t)=f(t)+g(t)+1$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 2.** $S(f)(t)+S(g)(t)=(f(t)+1)+(g(t)+1)=f(t)+g(t)+1$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 3.** The two agree, so $S$ is additive; it is linear.

:::Which step is wrong?
**Step 2.** $(f+1)+(g+1)=f+g+2$, not $f+g+1$. So $S(f+g)\neq S(f)+S(g)$ and $S$ is not additive. There is also a one-line check from the zero test: $S(0)(t)=0+1=1$ is the constant function $1$, not the zero function, so $S$ cannot be linear. It is an affine map (a translation in $C(\mathbb{R})$).
:::

parts.title: Is every vector a column of numbers?
parts.md: No. In this course a vector is any element of a vector space: a matrix in $M_{m\times n}$ or a function in $C(\mathbb{R})$ qualifies, because addition and scaling obey the same ten rules.

parts.title: If $T(0)=0$, is $T$ linear?
parts.md: Not necessarily. $T(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has $T(0)=0$, but $T(1+1)=4\neq T(1)+T(1)=2$. The zero test can only *refute* linearity.

parts.title: Why bother with function spaces?
parts.md: Many operations on functions are linear maps, for example differentiation on polynomials: $(af+bg)'=af'+bg'$. Treating functions as vectors lets the same tools apply to signals, polynomials and models.

parts.title: Does every linear map have a matrix?
parts.md: Every linear map $\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ has a standard matrix whose columns are $T(e_1),\dots,T(e_n)$. For other vector spaces you get a matrix after choosing a basis.

Test the ideas numerically. Build the standard matrix by applying the map to the columns of the identity, then test linearity numerically. ```html 
import numpy as np

def T(v):
    x, y = v
    return np.array([2*x - y, x + 3*y])

E = np.eye(2)
A = np.column_stack([T(E[:, j]) for j in range(2)])   # columns are T(e_j)
print(A)

v = np.array([1., 2.])
print("T(v) =", T(v), " A @ v =", A @ v)                # the same vector

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u, w = rng.normal(size=2), rng.normal(size=2)
a, b = 2.5, -1.5
print(np.allclose(T(a*u + b*w), a*T(u) + b*T(w)))      # T(au + bw) = aT(u) + bT(w)
``` **Output** ```html 
[[ 2. -1.]
 [ 1.  3.]]
T(v) = [0. 7.]  A @ v = [0. 7.]
True
``` A numerical test can **refute** linearity (one counterexample is enough) but it can never prove it: for a proof you need the algebra for all vectors. ```html 
import numpy as np

def R(v):                      # (x, y) -> (xy, x), not linear
    x, y = v
    return np.array([x*y, x])

def Tr(v):                     # translation (x, y) -> (x, y + 2), not linear
    x, y = v
    return np.array([x, y + 2])

zero = np.zeros(2)
print("R(0) =", R(zero), " Tr(0) =", Tr(zero))   # T(0) must be 0 for a linear map

u = np.array([1., 1.])
print("R(2u) =", R(2*u), " 2R(u) =", 2*R(u))     # homogeneity fails for R

A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 1.]])                # matrix of T(x, y) = (2x + y, x + y)
print("T^-1(3, 2) =", np.linalg.solve(A, [3., 2.]))
``` **Output** ```html 
R(0) = [0. 0.]  Tr(0) = [0. 2.]
R(2u) = [4. 2.]  2R(u) = [2. 2.]
T^-1(3, 2) = [1. 1.]
```

flashcards.title: Flashcards · Vector spaces and linear mappings

items.meaning: A nonempty set with addition and real scalar multiplication satisfying ten rules: closure under + and ·, commutativity, associativity, zero vector, additive inverses, two distributive laws, c(du) = (cd)u, 1u = u.
The vector 0 with u + 0 = u for every u. In C(ℝ) it is the function that is 0 for every t (not the constant 1).
ℝⁿ (componentwise), the space M(m × n) of matrices of a fixed shape, and the continuous functions C(ℝ) with pointwise operations.
A subset W is a subspace if it contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
items.example: {(x, y): x + y = 0} is a subspace; {(x, y): x + y = 1} is not (no zero).

items.meaning: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u); equivalently T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v).
Every linear map has T(0) = 0. If T(0) ≠ 0, T is not linear; if T(0) = 0 you still need to check both conditions.
items.example: T(x) = x + b with b ≠ 0 is not linear.

items.meaning: A = [T(e₁) … T(eₙ)]: the j-th column is the image of the j-th standard basis vector; T(x) = Ax.
x ↦ Ax + b. It is linear exactly when b = 0.
items.note: A neural-network layer Wx + b is affine.

items.meaning: The matrix of S ∘ T is BA (T acts first). T is invertible iff its matrix A is invertible, and the matrix of T⁻¹ is A⁻¹.

summary: A vector space is any set with addition and scalar multiplication obeying the ten axioms; Rⁿ, matrices of a fixed shape and continuous functions are examples.
A subset is a subspace if it contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; failing any one of the three means it is not.
A map is linear if T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u); every linear map sends 0 to 0, so T(0) ≠ 0 proves a map is not linear.
Every linear map Rⁿ → Rᵐ is x ↦ Ax with A = [T(e₁) … T(eₙ)]; the images of the basis vectors are the columns.
x ↦ Ax + b is affine and linear only if b = 0; composition corresponds to matrix products and T⁻¹ to A⁻¹.

quiz.title: Quiz · Vector Spaces and Linear Mappings

questions.explanation: Add component by component: $1+2=3$, $-2+4=2$ and $3+(-1)=2$. Addition in a vector space is not componentwise multiplication.

questions.prompt: What is the zero vector in the vector space $C(\mathbb{R})$ of continuous real functions?
questions.explanation: The zero vector must leave every function unchanged under pointwise addition: $f+0=f$. Only the function that is $0$ at every $t$ does that. The constant function $1$ would change $f$ into $f+1$.

questions.prompt: Let $T(x) = x + (1, -2)^\top$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which value of $T(0)$ shows that $T$ is not linear?
questions.explanation: Substituting gives $T(0)=0+(1,-2)^\top=(1,-2)^\top\neq 0$. Every linear map sends $0$ to $0$, so this translation fails a necessary condition and cannot be linear.

questions.prompt: For $f(t) = t^2$ and $g(t) = 1 - t$ in $C(\mathbb{R})$, what is $(2f - g)(t)$?
questions.explanation: Function operations are pointwise: $(2f-g)(t)=2t^2-(1-t)=2t^2-1+t=2t^2+t-1$. The minus sign applies to both terms of $g$.

questions.prompt: What is the standard matrix of $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$, $T(x, y) = (x + 2y,\ 3x - y)$?
questions.explanation: The first column is $T(1,0)=(1,3)^\top$ and the second is $T(0,1)=(2,-1)^\top$. Placing these as columns gives $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}$; writing them as rows gives the transpose (option C).

questions.prompt: Which map from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is linear?
questions.explanation: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ is multiplication by $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so it is linear. The translation $(x+1,y)$ fails $T(0)=0$; the square $(x^2,y)$ fails additivity; and the absolute value $(|x|,y)$ fails homogeneity for negative scalars.

questions.prompt: A linear map has $T(e_1) = (1, 2)^\top$, $T(e_2) = (-1, 3)^\top$. What is $T(2, -1)$?
questions.explanation: Linearity gives $T(2e_1-e_2)=2T(e_1)-T(e_2)=2(1,2)^\top-(-1,3)^\top=(2+1,\ 4-3)^\top=(3,1)^\top$. The negative coefficient applies to both coordinates of $T(e_2)$.

questions.prompt: On $C(\mathbb{R})$, define $(Sf)(t) = f(t) + f(0)$. Which function satisfies $(Sf)(t) = t^2 + 1$ for every real $t$?
questions.explanation: Evaluate at $t=0$: $2f(0)=1$, so $f(0)=\tfrac12$. Then $f(t)=t^2+1-f(0)=t^2+\tfrac12$. It is continuous, and $f(t)+f(0)=t^2+\tfrac12+\tfrac12=t^2+1$ for every $t$.

questions.prompt: A linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $T(1, 1) = 2(1, 1)$ and $T(1, -1) = -(1, -1)$. What is $T^{-1}(3, 1)$?
questions.explanation: The vectors $v_1=(1,1)$ and $v_2=(1,-1)$ are independent and $T$ multiplies them by the nonzero numbers $2$ and $-1$, so $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}$ divides by those numbers. Write $(3,1)=2v_1+v_2$. Then $T^{-1}(3,1)=\tfrac22v_1+\tfrac1{-1}v_2=v_1-v_2=(0,2)$. Check: $T(0,2)=T(v_1-v_2)=2v_1+v_2=(3,1)$. Option C is $T(3,1)$, the map applied instead of its inverse.

questions.prompt: The set $\{(x, y) : x \geq 0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
questions.explanation: False. It contains $0$ and is closed under addition, but not under scalar multiplication: $(-1)\cdot(1,0)=(-1,0)$ has $x\lt 0$. All three conditions must hold.

questions.prompt: Which subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a subspace?
questions.explanation: Only $x+y+z=0$ passes: it contains $0$, and sums and scalar multiples of solutions are again solutions. $x+y+z=1$ misses $0$; $z\geq0$ fails scaling by $-1$; $xyz=0$ (the union of the three coordinate planes) fails addition: $(1,1,0)+(0,0,1)=(1,1,1)$.

questions.prompt: $T:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is linear. Enter the shape of its standard matrix as $m\times n$.
questions.explanation: The standard matrix has one column $T(e_j)$ for each of the $3$ input coordinates, and each column has $2$ entries (it lies in $\mathbb{R}^2$). So the matrix is $2\times3$.

questions.prompt: $T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is linear with $T(e_1)=(1,0,2)^\top$ and $T(e_2)=(0,1,-1)^\top$. Enter the **third** coordinate of $T(3,-2)$.
questions.explanation: $T(3,-2)=3T(e_1)-2T(e_2)=3(1,0,2)-2(0,1,-1)=(3,-2,6+2)=(3,-2,8)$. The third coordinate is $8$. The negative coefficient applies to the whole vector $T(e_2)$, including its third coordinate $-1$.

questions.prompt: If $T(0)=0$, then $T$ is linear.
questions.explanation: False. $T(0)=0$ is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. $T(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has $T(0)=0$, yet $T(1+1)=4\neq T(1)+T(1)=2$. To prove linearity you must check additivity and homogeneity for all vectors.

misconceptions.name: Treats a product, power or function of the unknowns as linear
misconceptions.description: Calls an equation linear because it is an equation in x and y, even though an unknown is squared, multiplied by another unknown, or placed inside a function such as eˣ. An equation is linear only if each unknown appears to the first power, multiplied by a fixed number, and is only added to other terms.

misconceptions.name: Writes the augmented matrix with a wrong sign or column order
misconceptions.description: Transcribes a system into [A | b] with a sign changed, or with the columns in a different order from the declared unknowns. The first columns must hold the coefficients of x, y, … in that order and the last column must hold the right-hand sides with their signs.

misconceptions.name: Believes an operation that destroys information is an elementary row operation
misconceptions.description: Thinks that multiplying a row by zero, replacing a row by a copy of another, or swapping variable columns preserves the solution set. Only three operations are safe: swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero number, and add a multiple of one row to another. Each of these can be undone; the faulty ones cannot.

misconceptions.name: Carries out a row replacement incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Applies R2 ← R2 − 3R1 to only part of the row: leaves the right-hand side unchanged, forgets that the first entry changes too, or adds where it should subtract. A row operation acts on every entry of the row, including the entry after the bar.

misconceptions.name: Misreads a row of zeros in an augmented matrix
misconceptions.description: Reads a row [0 0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0 as harmless or as meaning infinitely many solutions, or reads the row [0 0 0 | 0] as a contradiction. The first says 0 = c, which is impossible; the second says 0 = 0, which is always true.

misconceptions.name: Checks or substitutes carelessly
misconceptions.description: Back-substitutes with a missing coefficient (x = 7 − y instead of x = 7 − 2y) or verifies a candidate in only some equations. A vector is a solution only if it satisfies every equation of the system.

misconceptions.name: Loses a sign or a variable when writing the general solution
misconceptions.description: Moves a free-variable term across the equals sign without changing its sign (x1 + 2x3 = 3 gives x1 = 3 − 2t, not 3 + 2t), or ignores that the free variable also appears in the other equations. Spanning vectors proposed for a solution set must themselves satisfy the equations.

misconceptions.name: Assumes a system with a parameter behaves the same for every value
misconceptions.description: Treats a system containing a parameter a as having one type of solution for all a. Elimination produces factors such as (a − 2); at the value that makes such a factor vanish, a pivot disappears and the number of solutions changes (unique, none or infinitely many).

misconceptions.name: Misjudges how many solutions a system has
misconceptions.description: Counts solutions by the number of unknowns, thinks a homogeneous system can have no solution or only the zero solution regardless of shape, or thinks fewer equations than unknowns can still give a unique solution. Uniqueness needs a pivot in every variable column; if there are more unknowns than pivots, a consistent system has infinitely many solutions.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up the shape rules for addition and multiplication
misconceptions.description: Believes A + B is defined whenever the shapes are 'similar' (same number of rows, or same number of entries), or gives the shape of AB as swapped or as the inner dimensions. Addition needs identical shapes. For multiplication the inner dimensions must agree and the result has the outer dimensions: (m × k)(k × n) is m × n.

misconceptions.name: Applies a scalar to only some entries or changes its sign
misconceptions.description: Multiplies only the diagonal (or one row) of a matrix by a scalar, or uses +c instead of −c. In cA every entry is multiplied by c.

misconceptions.name: Pairs the wrong entries in a matrix product
misconceptions.description: Multiplies matching entries (entrywise product) or uses the wrong row or column. The entry (AB)ij is the sum of products of row i of A with column j of B.

misconceptions.name: Assumes AB = BA
misconceptions.description: Treats matrix multiplication like multiplication of numbers and swaps the factors freely. In general AB ≠ BA, and one of the products may not even be defined.

misconceptions.name: Transposes incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Leaves the matrix unchanged, reverses the entries, rotates it, or forgets to transpose when combining rules. The transpose turns row i into column i, so an m × n matrix becomes n × m.

misconceptions.name: Misremembers the 2 × 2 inverse formula
misconceptions.description: Forgets the factor 1/(ad − bc), keeps the signs of the off-diagonal entries, or does not swap the diagonal entries. For [[a,b],[c,d]] the inverse is 1/(ad − bc) · [[d, −b],[−c, a]].

misconceptions.name: Keeps the original order when transposing or inverting a product
misconceptions.description: Writes (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ or (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹, or treats the inverse of a sum as the sum of inverses. Both rules reverse the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

misconceptions.name: Mishandles a scalar factor inside an inverse
misconceptions.description: Writes (cA)⁻¹ = cA⁻¹ instead of c⁻¹A⁻¹, or drops the scalar altogether. Inverting reciprocates the scalar.

misconceptions.name: Solves a matrix equation by multiplying on the wrong side or by the wrong matrix
misconceptions.description: In AXB = I multiplies by A and B instead of A⁻¹ and B⁻¹, or multiplies both factors on the same side. To isolate X you must multiply on the left by A⁻¹ and on the right by B⁻¹, and the order matters.

misconceptions.name: Cancels a matrix factor as if it were a nonzero number
misconceptions.description: From AB = AC concludes B = C. This is valid only if A is invertible (multiply by A⁻¹); otherwise B and C can differ.

misconceptions.name: Uses the wrong formula for a 2 × 2 determinant
misconceptions.description: Adds the diagonal products, or takes only one product, instead of computing ad − bc. The determinant is the main-diagonal product minus the other-diagonal product.

misconceptions.name: Forgets the checkerboard sign or deletes the wrong row and column
misconceptions.description: Takes the minor as the cofactor, or deletes the wrong row or column when forming the minor. The cofactor is Cij = (−1)^(i+j) · Mij, where Mij comes from deleting row i and column j.

misconceptions.name: Does not take the product of the diagonal of a triangular matrix
misconceptions.description: Adds the diagonal entries, drops a sign, or thinks an entry of 0 anywhere makes the determinant 0. For a triangular matrix det A is the product of the diagonal entries, signs included.

misconceptions.name: Misjudges how row operations change the determinant
misconceptions.description: Forgets that a row swap changes the sign, that scaling a row by c multiplies the determinant by c, or thinks that adding a multiple of one row to another changes the determinant. Replacement leaves it unchanged.

misconceptions.name: Treats the determinant as if it were linear
misconceptions.description: Writes det(A + B) = det A + det B, or det(cA) = c·det A. The determinant is multiplicative (det AB = det A · det B), and scaling an n × n matrix by c multiplies the determinant by cⁿ.

misconceptions.name: Misapplies a determinant rule for inverses, products or the adjoint
misconceptions.description: Uses the wrong sign or exponent in det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, det(A²) = (det A)², det(Aᵀ) = det A, or det(adj A) = (det A)ⁿ⁻¹. A single wrong sign changes the final answer.

misconceptions.name: Thinks det A = 0 means Ax = b never has a solution
misconceptions.description: Confuses 'A is not invertible' with 'the system is inconsistent'. If det A = 0 then Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many, depending on b.

misconceptions.name: Pairs an eigenvector with an eigenvalue it does not belong to
misconceptions.description: Chooses an eigenvalue or eigenvector without checking Av = λv for that pair. A vector can be an eigenvector for one eigenvalue and still fail the equation for another.

misconceptions.name: Adds conditions to the definition of an eigenvector or eigenvalue
misconceptions.description: Requires the eigenvalue to be nonzero, the eigenvector to have length one, or all its coordinates to be nonzero. The definition needs only v ≠ 0 and Av = λv; λ = 0 is allowed and happens exactly when A is singular.

misconceptions.name: Misreads the eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix
misconceptions.description: Invents an eigenvalue, drops a sign, or takes absolute values. The eigenvalues of a diagonal (or triangular) matrix are exactly its diagonal entries, with their signs.

misconceptions.name: Gets the eigenvalue of A⁻¹ wrong
misconceptions.description: Thinks A⁻¹ has the same eigenvalue as A, or its negative, or its square. If Av = λv with λ ≠ 0 then A⁻¹v = (1/λ)v.

misconceptions.name: Orders the diagonal entries differently from the eigenvector columns
misconceptions.description: Builds P from eigenvectors but writes the eigenvalues in D in another order. In A = PDP⁻¹ the j-th diagonal entry of D must be the eigenvalue of the j-th column of P.

misconceptions.name: Misjudges when a matrix is diagonalizable
misconceptions.description: Thinks a repeated eigenvalue always rules out diagonalization (or always allows it), or counts eigenvalues instead of independent eigenvectors. A is diagonalizable over ℝ exactly when it has n linearly independent real eigenvectors.

misconceptions.name: Mishandles powers or polynomials of a matrix
misconceptions.description: Slips when computing an entry of Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ (wrong factor, wrong row or column of P or P⁻¹), or forgets that p(A)v = p(λ)v, so that (for a diagonalizable A) the kernel of p(A) is spanned by the eigenvectors whose eigenvalues are roots of p.

misconceptions.name: Slips in componentwise, pointwise or linear-combination arithmetic
misconceptions.description: Subtracts instead of adds, multiplies instead of adds, loses the sign of a subtracted function, or applies a negative coefficient to only one coordinate. Vector spaces add componentwise (or pointwise for functions).

misconceptions.name: Confuses the additive identity with the multiplicative identity
misconceptions.description: In a function space picks the constant function 1, or another function, as the zero vector. The zero vector is the function that is 0 for every t, because it is the only one that leaves every function unchanged under pointwise addition.

misconceptions.name: Misuses the test T(0) = 0
misconceptions.description: Does not know that every linear map sends 0 to 0 (so T(0) ≠ 0 proves non-linearity), computes T(0) incorrectly, or treats T(0) = 0 as enough to prove linearity. T(0) = 0 is necessary but not sufficient.

misconceptions.name: Builds the standard matrix incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Writes the images T(e1), T(e2), … as rows instead of columns, swaps the columns, or loses a sign. The standard matrix is A = [T(e1) … T(en)]: the j-th column is the image of ej.

misconceptions.name: Believes a map such as a translation, absolute value or square is linear
misconceptions.description: Treats a map as linear because it 'looks simple'. A translation fails T(0) = 0; squaring fails additivity; the absolute value fails homogeneity for negative scalars.

misconceptions.name: Applies T instead of T⁻¹, or solves an operator equation carelessly
misconceptions.description: To invert a linear map applies the map itself, forgets to reciprocate the eigenvalues, or ignores that a constant such as f(0) is itself unknown. The inverse of T undoes T.

misconceptions.name: Applies only part of the subspace test
misconceptions.description: Checks that a set contains 0, or that it is closed under addition, and stops. A subset is a subspace only if it contains 0 and is closed under both addition and scalar multiplication.

feedbackTemplates.body: A linear equation may contain only terms of the form (number) × (unknown). A product such as xy, a power such as x², or a function such as eˣ or sin x makes the equation nonlinear, no matter how simple it looks. Test each term: is it a fixed number times a single unknown? If yes for every term, the equation is linear.

Read the system equation by equation: column 1 is always the coefficient of the first unknown, column 2 of the second, and the last column after the bar holds the right-hand sides. Check every entry against its equation, signs included; swapping columns changes which unknown each column belongs to, so it changes the system.

A row operation is safe only if you can undo it. Multiplying a row by 0 or overwriting it with a copy of another row throws an equation away, so you cannot get it back, and the solution set can grow. Swapping variable columns relabels the unknowns, which changes the system. Stick to the three legal operations: swap rows, scale a row by c ≠ 0, add a multiple of one row to another.

A row operation acts on the whole row, the right-hand side included. For R2 ← R2 − 3R1 compute every entry of the new row 2 as (old entry of row 2) − 3 × (entry of row 1 in the same column), then keep row 1 unchanged. If the entry in the pivot column does not become 0, something went wrong.

Translate the row back into an equation. [0 0 0 | 4] says 0·x + 0·y + 0·z = 4, that is 0 = 4, which no values of the unknowns can satisfy, so the system is inconsistent. Only a row [0 0 0 | 0] (the equation 0 = 0) is harmless. The right-hand entry decides.

A solution must satisfy all equations at once. Substitute the candidate into every equation, not just the first one, and keep the coefficients when you back-substitute: in x + 2y = 7 with y = 2, the term is 2y = 4, so x = 3. Several wrong answers satisfy one equation and fail another.

Solve each pivot equation for its basic variable. From x1 + 2x3 = 3 and x3 = t you get x1 = 3 − 2t: the term 2t moves to the right with its sign flipped. Then substitute your final family back into every original equation for a few values of t. A correct general solution passes for all t.

After elimination, look at every entry that you would need to divide by. Where it contains the parameter, such as (a − 2)y = 0, split into cases: if the factor is nonzero you can divide and get a pivot; if it is zero the pivot is lost and you must read the row again (0 = 0 means a free variable, 0 = c ≠ 0 means no solution). Then check each special value separately.

Count pivots. A unique solution needs a pivot in every variable column, so you need at least as many equations as unknowns. If a system has more unknowns than equations and is consistent, a free variable exists and there are infinitely many solutions. A homogeneous system Ax = 0 is always consistent (x = 0 works), so with more unknowns than equations it has infinitely many solutions.

Write the shapes side by side. For A + B the two shapes must be identical, so a 2 × 3 matrix needs a 2 × 3 partner. For AB write (m × k)(k × n): the two inner numbers must match, and the result takes the outer numbers, m × n. Do this check before computing a single entry.

Scalar multiplication is entry by entry: (cA)ij = c·aij for every i and j, zeros included. For −2A multiply each entry by −2, so −3 becomes 6 and 2 becomes −4. Check that no entry has been skipped and that no sign has been lost.

(AB)ij is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: add the products ai1·b1j + ai2·b2j + … . Multiplying matching entries (as numpy's * does) is a different operation. Write out which row and which column you are using before you multiply.

Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Taking A = [[1,2],[0,1]] and B = [[2,0],[1,3]], AB has first row (4, 6) but BA has first row (2, 4). The order of the factors tells you which transformation acts first, so always keep it.

The transpose turns rows into columns: row 1 of A becomes column 1 of Aᵀ, row 2 becomes column 2, and so on. The shape changes from m × n to n × m, and (Aᵀ)ij = aji. Check the shape first, then fill in column by column from the rows of A.

For a 2 × 2 matrix swap the two diagonal entries, change the sign of the two off-diagonal entries, and divide everything by ad − bc. Always verify by multiplying A by your answer: you should get the identity. If the upper-right entry of the product is not 0, a sign is wrong.

Transposes and inverses of a product reverse the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. Think of putting on socks (A) then shoes (B): to undo it you remove the shoes first. Also, there is no rule for the inverse of a sum: (A + B)⁻¹ is generally not A⁻¹ + B⁻¹.
The inverse of cA undoes multiplication by c, so it contains 1/c: (cA)⁻¹ = (1/c)·A⁻¹. Combine this with (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ step by step and check by multiplying your answer with the original matrix.

To isolate X in AXB = I, multiply on the left by A⁻¹ and on the right by B⁻¹: X = A⁻¹·I·B⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹. Do not multiply by A or B themselves, and do not swap the sides. Verify by computing AXB and checking that you get I.

You may cancel A from AB = AC only by multiplying both sides by A⁻¹, which needs A to be invertible. If A is singular this fails: A = [[1,0],[0,0]] sends both [[1,1],[1,1]] and [[1,1],[2,2]] to the same matrix [[1,1],[0,0]]. Matrices are not numbers.

For [[a,b],[c,d]] the determinant is ad − bc: multiply along the main diagonal, multiply along the other diagonal, then subtract. Adding the products (ad + bc) or stopping after one product are common slips.

Two checks. First, delete exactly row i and column j to form the minor Mij. Second, multiply by (−1)^(i+j): positions with i + j even keep the sign of the minor, positions with i + j odd flip it. For position (1, 2) the sign is −1, so a minor of −6 gives a cofactor of +6.

For an upper or lower triangular matrix the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries, not the sum, and the signs count: 2 · (−1) · 5 = −10. Entries off the diagonal play no role. (Cofactor expansion along the first column explains why.)

Track each operation: swapping two rows multiplies det by −1; multiplying one row by c multiplies det by c; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged. Apply them in order, starting from the original determinant, and do not count a replacement as a change.

The determinant is not additive: with A = B = I₂ you have det(A + B) = det(2I) = 4 but det A + det B = 2. For scaling, every one of the n rows is multiplied by c, so det(cA) = cⁿ det A. The rule that does hold for products is det(AB) = det A · det B.

List the facts you need and write each factor separately: det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, det(Aᵀ) = det A, det(A²) = (det A)², det(adj A) = (det A)ⁿ⁻¹ for an n × n matrix. Multiply the factors at the end and watch the signs, because det B can be negative.

When det A = 0 there is no unique solution, but a particular system Ax = b can still have solutions: it is inconsistent for some b and has infinitely many solutions for others. For A = [[1,2],[2,4]], Ax = (3, 6) has infinitely many solutions while Ax = (3, 7) has none.

Always test the pair: compute Av and compare with λv. For a given λ the eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of (A − λI)v = 0, so solve that system for the λ you were given, and check your vector in the original equation Av = λv.

The definition has two conditions: v ≠ 0 and Av = λv. Length one is a convenient normalisation, not a requirement; coordinates may be zero; and λ = 0 is a legitimate eigenvalue, which occurs precisely when A is singular. Do not add conditions that are not in the definition.

For a diagonal matrix, each standard basis vector ej is an eigenvector and its eigenvalue is the j-th diagonal entry, signs included. So diag(−2, 0, 5) has eigenvalues −2, 0 and 5 and nothing else. Read the diagonal, do not compute anything else.
Start from Av = λv and multiply by A⁻¹: v = λA⁻¹v, so A⁻¹v = (1/λ)v. The eigenvector stays the same and the eigenvalue becomes its reciprocal, sign included: for λ = −2 you get −1/2, not 1/2 or 4.

From AP = PD, column j of P is multiplied by dj, so dj must be the eigenvalue belonging to column j. Reordering the columns of P forces the same reordering of D. If you are unsure, test the first column: A·p1 must equal d1·p1.

Do not decide from the eigenvalues alone: count independent eigenvectors. A repeated eigenvalue can still give a full eigenvector basis (2I) or not ([[2,1],[0,2]]). For each eigenvalue solve (A − λI)v = 0 and see how many independent solutions you get; you need n in total.

Use Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ and pick out the entry by multiplying the right row of P, the diagonal Dᵏ and the right column of P⁻¹; then check the formula at k = 1, where you must get the original entry. For p(A)v = 0 look at the eigenvalues: when A has an eigenvector basis, exactly the eigenvectors whose eigenvalue is a root of p are sent to 0.

In ℝⁿ add component by component; for functions add pointwise, (f + g)(t) = f(t) + g(t). When you subtract, the minus sign applies to the whole of the second object: 2f − g subtracts every term of g. For linear combinations, a coefficient multiplies every coordinate of the vector it belongs to.

The zero vector 0 satisfies u + 0 = u for every u. In C(ℝ) addition is pointwise, so the zero vector must add nothing at every t: it is the function f(t) = 0. The constant function 1 is the identity for multiplication of functions, which is not an operation of the vector space.

Every linear map satisfies T(0) = T(0·0) = 0·T(0) = 0. So if T(0) ≠ 0, the map is not linear, as for a translation. The converse is false: T(x) = x² has T(0) = 0 but is not linear. To prove linearity check additivity and homogeneity for all vectors.

The j-th column of the standard matrix is T(ej). Compute T(1, 0) and T(0, 1) from the formula and write each result as a column. Then test the matrix: A·(x, y)ᵀ must reproduce the formula for T(x, y).

Test the two conditions with specific numbers. x + 1 fails because T(0) ≠ 0. x² fails additivity: (1 + 1)² = 4 but 1² + 1² = 2. |x| fails homogeneity: |−1 · 1| = 1 but −1 · |1| = −1. A map is linear only if both conditions hold for all vectors and scalars.

To find T⁻¹(w) solve T(v) = w, and then verify by applying T to your answer: you should get w back. In an eigenbasis, T acts as multiplication by λ on each eigenvector, so T⁻¹ divides by λ. For operators like (Sf)(t) = f(t) + f(0), evaluate at t = 0 first to find the unknown constant f(0).

The subspace test has three parts: contains 0, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiplication. A set can pass two and fail one. {(x, y): x ≥ 0} contains 0 and is closed under addition but fails scaling: −1 · (1, 0) = (−1, 0) leaves the set.

Re-read the definition in this topic and rework the question on paper, checking each step with a small example. Rating your confidence before the answer will tell you whether this was a slip or a gap.
